football_evidence.question: Can Wisconsin take away USC’s big plays?
football_evidence.assessment: Most of the 4.7-point difference traces to home field (engine constant) (about 1.6 points), which the closing market has historically priced differently. That explains the gap; it does not make either number a bet.
supporting: When Wisconsin has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Wisconsin’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 11.6% of its runs, and USC’s defense stops 14.8% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.3%).

When USC has the ball (big plays on the ground): USC’s offense turns 4.4% of its runs into explosive gains, and Wisconsin’s defense gives up explosive gains on 2.6% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

When Wisconsin has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Wisconsin’s offense has allowed a sack on 3.7% of its dropbacks, and USC’s defense sacks the quarterback on 5.5% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).
When USC has the ball (the run game against the run defense): USC’s offense averages 4.9 yards per carry, and Wisconsin’s defense allows 3.6 yards per carry (FBS average 5.1).
contradicting: When Wisconsin has the ball (big plays on the ground): Wisconsin’s offense turns 4.8% of its runs into explosive gains, and USC’s defense gives up explosive gains on 3.4% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

Jayden Maiava has completed 152 of 225 passes (67.6%) for 2,045 yards, 9.1 yards per attempt, 18 touchdowns and 3 interceptions in seven games for USC, and has been sacked on 6 of 231 dropbacks.
Jonas Williams has completed 12 of 14 passes (85.7%) for 126 yards, 9.0 yards per attempt, no touchdowns and 1 interception in three games for USC, and has been sacked on 1 of 15 dropbacks.
